title: When quality beats cheap, and when it does not
description: Some things are worth paying more for because they last; others are identical under the label, and knowing which is which saves twice.

body.heading: Pay more where wear happens
paragraphs: Items that face daily friction repay quality: shoes worn every day, a coat for a wet climate, a mattress, tools you use weekly, a school bag dragged through three winters. For these, the honest measure is cost per use, and a well-made item used five hundred times beats a cheap one replaced five times.
Quality also tends to be repairable. A stitched sole can be resoled and a wooden chair reglued, while the glued-together bargain often cannot be fixed at all.

body.heading: Save where the difference is invisible
paragraphs: Basic ingredients, cleaning staples, plain stationery and many store-brand foods are made to the same standards as famous labels, sometimes in the same factories. Here the premium buys packaging and advertising, and the savings from switching are real and repeatable.

The test is simple: if you cannot tell the difference in a fair trial, there is no difference worth paying for. Run the trial once, honestly, and then buy the cheaper version without a second thought.

body.heading: Beware the middle trap
paragraphs: The worst value often sits in the middle: priced like quality, built like the bargain. Price alone is not evidence of durability, so look for the signs instead: materials you can identify, solid construction, spare parts and a maker willing to guarantee the work.
Reviews from people who have owned the item for years are worth more than first impressions. Longevity leaves a paper trail, if you look for it.

takeaway: Spend up on things that wear, save on things that are identical, and judge by construction and cost per use, not by price.
